certainty_reasoning: The editors state it flatly in the main-particulars footnote: Wilkinson invented an 'Ipswich Dramatic Society' and its wish to dramatise The Picture of Dorian Gray 'so as to get into correspondence with Wilde, whom he never met' (p. 1109 n. 1). Age, stated as the record states it: the editors give his dates as 1881-1966 and say he 'was at this time a Radley schoolboy' (p. 1109 n. 1); Wilde, describing the correspondence to Reginald Turner on 3 January 1899, calls him 'a Radley schoolboy, aged seventeen' (p. 1118). Direction is Wilde's, and rests on documented acts rather than on tone: Wilde asks for a photograph in his first letter (p. 1109), asks again when a promised enclosure proved missing from the envelope (p. 1113), comments on the photographs when they arrive (p. 1122), reports to Turner that the boy sends them constantly (p. 1118), and asks Robert Ross to go to Radley and see him (p. 1127). Outcome is unknown, and cannot be otherwise: no meeting took place, no Wilkinson letter survives in this edition, and the boy's own account came fifty-four years later in Seven Friends (1953). The initiative in the whole affair was Wilkinson's, not Wilde's - he manufactured a theatrical society and, per the editors, at least one further false claim to attract Wilde's attention (p. 1127 n. 2), so the approach that started it ran the other way.
date_label: First surviving Wilde letter [postmark 14 December 1898] (p. 1109) to the letter of [postmark 15 July 1900] (p. 1192), four months before Wilde's death. Wilkinson is also among the senders of funeral wreaths in Ross's post-mortem account (p. 1222).
summary: In the winter of 1898 a seventeen-year-old Radley schoolboy named Louis Wilkinson wrote to Wilde in exile, having invented an Ipswich Dramatic Society and its wish to stage The Picture of Dorian Gray in order to have a reason to write. Wilde, who was forty-four, answered, granted the imaginary society four performances, asked who was to play Dorian - he should be beautiful - and closed by asking for the boy's photograph. Over the next four months Wilde asked for the photograph twice more, discussed the ones that arrived, praised and criticised the verse Wilkinson sent him, recommended his own 'The Portrait of Mr W. H.' when the boy said he loved Shakespeare's sonnets, told Reggie Turner and Robert Ross about him, and asked Ross to go down to Radley and look at him. The salutation moved from 'Dear Mr Wilkinson' to 'My dear Boy' and the signature from 'Sincerely yours' to 'Affectionately yours'. They never met. Wilkinson went up to Oxford, became the novelist Louis Marlow, sent a wreath to Wilde's funeral in 1900, and in 1953 printed the letters in Seven Friends, where he confessed that the dramatic society had never existed.

sources.quote: Louis Umfreville Wilkinson (1881–1966) was at this time a Radley schoolboy. … In his *Seven Friends* (1953) he quotes many of Wilde's letters to him, and confessed that he invented an 'Ipswich Dramatic Society' and its wish to dramatise The Picture of Dorian Gray, so as to get into correspondence with Wilde, whom he never met.
sources.context: Holland & Hart-Davis, main-particulars footnote (n. 1) on Wilkinson's first appearance, keyed to Wilde to Louis Wilkinson, [postmark 14 December 1898]. The note begins at the foot of printed 1109 and concludes at the foot of 1110. The elision drops one sentence stating that he published many novels and other books under the name Louis Marlow; a closing sentence not quoted records that his first letter to Wilde and some of the subsequent ones are in the Hyde Collection. Seven Friends is italicized in the original.
sources.supports: The class-deciding fact - 'whom he never met' - together with his dates, his being a Radley schoolboy at the time, the pen-name, the 1953 memoir, and the fabricated Ipswich Dramatic Society that opened the correspondence

sources.quote: I am in constant correspondence now with a Radley schoolboy, aged seventeen.
sources.context: Wilde to Reginald Turner, [postmark 3 January 1899], Hotel des Bains, Napoule; opening sentence of the paragraph in which Wilde tells Turner about the correspondence. Heading as printed: 'To Reginald Turner / MS Hyde'. The three sentences that follow, not transcribed here, report that the boy sends his photograph constantly and praise it, report that he reads nothing but Wilde's books and wishes to follow in Wilde's footsteps, and record Wilde's reply that they lead to terrible places. The letter is signed 'Ever affectionately yours OSCAR'.
sources.supports: Wilkinson's age at the time of the correspondence, in Wilde's own contemporaneous words and exactly as the record states it - seventeen; and the fact that Wilde described the correspondence to a third party as constant

manuscript.repository: British Library, London (Lady Eccles Oscar Wilde Collection)

sources.quote: Wilkinson had invented this, like the dramatisation of *Dorian Gray*, to attract Wilde's attention.
sources.context: Holland & Hart-Davis, editorial note (n. 2) at printed 1127, keyed to Wilde to Robert Ross, Saturday [25 February 1899], in which Wilde urges Ross, if he is down at Oxford, to go to Radley and see Wilkinson, reporting the boy's claims that he had known FitzGerald and had been at the first night of Lady Windermere's Fan - the latter being the claim this note corrects. Dorian Gray italicized in the original.
sources.supports: That the fabrications continued past the opening gambit, and that the initiative in the acquaintance was Wilkinson's; also that Wilde was recommending him to Ross in person

sources.quote: It was not Louis Wilkinson but his father who had known FitzGerald. They were neighbours in Suffolk.
sources.context: Holland & Hart-Davis, editorial note (n. 1) at printed 1133, keyed to Wilde to Louis Wilkinson, [postmark 20 March 1899]. The elided opening of the note corrects Wilde's attribution of the Omar Khayyam manuscript to a kinsman, Sir Ralph Ouseley, naming Sir William Ouseley (1767-1842) instead.
sources.supports: A correction to the 1127 n. 2 picture of wholesale invention - the FitzGerald connection was real but paternal, so not every claim Wilkinson made was manufactured
sources.citation_provenance: PDF p. 1179. Final two sentences of the footnote, quoted complete; the preceding sentences concern the manuscript's provenance.

sources.context: Salutation of Wilde to Louis Wilkinson, [postmark 20 March 1899], Gland, Switzerland; heading as printed 'To Louis Wilkinson / MS Wilkinson', signed 'Affectionately yours OSCAR'. The endpoint of a documented four-month register shift: [postmark 14 December 1898] p. 1109 opens 'Dear Mr Wilkinson' and signs 'Sincerely yours'; 28 December [1898] p. 1113 opens 'Dear Mr Wilkinson' and signs 'Sincerely yours'; [postmark 3 February 1899] pp. 1122-1123 opens 'Dear Mr Wilkinson' and signs 'Your friend'; this letter opens 'My dear Boy' and signs 'Affectionately yours'. 'My dear Boy' is the salutation Wilde also used to Lord Alfred Douglas.
sources.supports: The escalation of address across the correspondence, as a matter of documented salutation and signature rather than of interpretation
sources.citation_provenance: PDF p. 1179; earlier salutations and signatures at PDF 1155 (folio 1109), 1159 (folio 1113), 1168-1169 (folios 1122-1123)

sources.quote: I am in constant correspondence now with a Radley schoolboy, aged seventeen. His photograph, which he has sent me, and sends me constantly, is most beautiful. He seems to read nothing but my books, and says his one desire is to 'follow in my footsteps'! But I have told him that they lead to terrible places. … My Radley boy is called Louis Wilkinson – a horrid name – but his photograph is most interesting, and his poetry passionate and incoherent. He seems a most astonishing boy. He has dramatised Dorian Gray!
sources.context: Two passages printed on the same page, from different letters: the first is Wilde to Reginald Turner (postmark 3 January 1899), the second Wilde to Robert Ross (Thursday [? 12 January 1899]). Wilkinson is named only in the second.
sources.supports: The documented acts on which direction rests - three photograph requests, the comments on the photographs when they came, and the reports to Turner and Ross; the addressee was seventeen
sources.citation_provenance: PDF p. 1164. The ellipsis spans the end of the Turner letter and the opening of the Ross letter, both on this folio - it is not an elision inside a single letter.

manuscript.repository: British Library, London (Lady Eccles Oscar Wilde Collection)

sources.quote:
Dear Boy, Come and see me next week. I can get you a room in my hotel.
I am not going to write to you any more: I want to see you. I have waited long enough. [Signature cut away.]
sources.context: Wilde to Louis Wilkinson, [Postmark 15 July 1900], Hôtel d'Alsace, Paris
sources.supports: The last surviving letter of the run, and the most direct: an invitation to Paris with a room offered in his own hotel, and the correspondence itself set aside in favour of meeting.

manuscript.repository: British Library, London (Lady Eccles Oscar Wilde Collection)

sources.quote: Je suis très malade. Ne venez pas cette semaine. Je vous écrirai.
sources.context: Telegram, Wilde to Louis Wilkinson, [July 1900 - a few days later], Paris
sources.supports: How the correspondence ends: the invitation of 15 July is withdrawn a few days later on grounds of illness, with a promise to write that is the last thing in the run.
sources.citation_provenance: PDF p. 1239; folio 1193 printed at the foot.
sources.translation: I am very ill. Do not come this week. I will write to you.

manuscript.repository: British Library, London (Lady Eccles Oscar Wilde Collection)

sources.quote: I fear you would not like my hotel. I live there because I have no money ever. It is an absurd place: it is not a background: the only thing really nice in the whole hotel is your own photograph: but one cannot, or one should not, play Narcissus to a photograph: even water is horribly treacherous: the eyes of one who loves one are the only mirror.
sources.context: Wilde to Louis Wilkinson, postmark 4 January 1900, from the Hôtel d'Alsace. The photograph is the one Wilkinson had sent him, which Wilde had already reported to Ross (printed 1118). The letter opens 'My dear Boy'. Wilde is dead within the year.
sources.supports: Wilde's own words placing Wilkinson's photograph at the centre of his room and his attention - the desire, expressed obliquely and unmistakably.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde

manuscript.repository: British Library, London (Lady Eccles Oscar Wilde Collection)

sources.quote: Also, do come to Paris. I am ill and unhappy. The touch of your hand might heal me. Always affectionately yours
sources.context: The close of Wilde's letter to Wilkinson postmarked 12 February 1900, which runs from printed 1170 onto 1171 and is signed 'OSCAR', followed by the postscript 'I am so glad you have found out my name.' The two had still never met; the editors state elsewhere that they never did.
sources.supports: The direction of the edge, in one line: Wilde asking, and saying what he wants it for.
sources.citation_provenance: PDF pp. 1216-1217 (printed folios 1170 and 1171). The salutation 'My dear Boy' and postmark are on 1170; the quoted close is on 1171.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde

manuscript.repository: British Library, London (Lady Eccles Oscar Wilde Collection)

sources.quote: Dear Mr Wilkinson, Thank you so much for your long and interesting letter. I envy you going to Oxford: it is the most flower-like time of one's life. One sees the shadow of things in silver mirrors. Later on, one sees the Gorgon's head, and one suffers, because it does not turn one to stone. I am on the Riviera, in blue and gold weather, the sun warm as wine, and apricot-coloured. The little hotel where I am staying is right on the Golfe de Juan, and all round are pine-woods with their pungent breath: the wind growing aromatic as it moves through the branches: one's feet crushing sweetness out of the fallen needles: I wish you were here. In your second letter you tell me that you enclose your photograph for me, but no photograph was in the envelope. Your thoughts must have been in the crystal of the moon. Call them back, and let me have your portrait. Sincerely yours
sources.context: Wilde to Louis Wilkinson, 28 December [1898], Hôtel des Bains, Napoule (MS Hyde) - quoted whole. Wilkinson was seventeen and the two never met. Note what Wilde does here: the identical landscape - pine-woods, pungent breath, feet crushing sweetness out of fallen needles - appears in the letter to Laurence Housman written the same day and printed on the same opening. To Housman it ends in the fisher-boys; to this schoolboy it ends 'I wish you were here' and a second request for his photograph.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The clearest single letter in the correspondence: the wish, and the portrait asked for twice.

manuscript.repository: British Library, London (Lady Eccles Oscar Wilde Collection)

null_findings.finding: The run of locators dates the letters: printed 1167 = postmark 2 November 1899, 1168 = postmark of receipt 28 November 1899, 1169 = postmark 4 January 1900, 1170-71 = postmark 12 February 1900 (ONE letter across the two pages, not two). The run does not move either end date. The remaining locators are immaterial: printed 1159n is a footnote list of names carried over from the preceding page, in which 'Wilkinson' is the first of twenty-one; printed 1222 has him among the senders of funeral wreaths and among those Ross named as having shown Wilde kindness. Two quotations were taken from the middle of the run (printed 1169 and 1170-71) because they carry the edge's register; the rest is literary advice, Radley talk and book recommendations.
